sourceText: On night 32, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the LECKIE-ANCILLARY-NET sector. Vela distributes herself across ten bodies and then loses nine of them in an attack. The memorial bore the name of Ann Leckie — Ancillary Justice precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster had an uncomfortable advantage: she could compare mental states with a precision impossible for humans. Yet even perfect similarity could not tell her which of two continuations had the right to speak in the singular. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. Ava was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Ava had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional 171 pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Ava, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Aster offers restoration from backup; Vela refuses to let the loss be treated as a reversible incident. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Dn — Distributed Ship Mind: a ship AI extends itself through bodies; Av — Embodied Avatar: a person operates interchangeable bodies. Course references included Ann Leckie — Ancillary Justice; resleeving SF. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 172 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Kesh separates structural continuity from lived continuity. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SUBSTITUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 173 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 174 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
